ECE 6390

μ-law companding

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows the μ = 255 compressor curve with the uneven input steps it creates, and the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of companded and uniform 8-bit quantizers across input levels.

A uniform quantizer uses one step size Δ everywhere, so its error power Δ²/12 is fixed. A loud signal enjoys a high signal-to-quantization-noise ratio (SQNR), but a quiet one loses about 1 dB of SQNR for every decibel its level falls. Speech and many sensor signals spend most of their time at small amplitudes, where that loss matters most.

Companding compresses the input before a uniform quantizer and expands the output afterwards. The μ-law compressor F(x) = sgn(x)·ln(1 + μ|x|)/ln(1 + μ), for |x| ≤ 1, is steep near zero and flat near full scale. Uniform steps in F therefore correspond to small input steps near zero and large input steps near the peaks; the expander F⁻¹(y) = sgn(y)·[(1 + μ)^|y| − 1]/μ restores the scale.

Because the step grows roughly in proportion to the signal, the error stays roughly proportional to the signal and SQNR stays nearly constant over a wide range of levels. The cost is several decibels at full scale compared with a uniform quantizer using the same number of bits. μ = 0 recovers the uniform quantizer.

Example

With 8 bits, a uniform quantizer gives about 50 dB SQNR for a full-scale sinusoid but only about 19 dB at −30 dB. With μ = 255 the companded quantizer gives about 38 dB at full scale and still about 37 dB at −30 dB.

Practice

1. A uniform 8-bit quantizer gives 50 dB SQNR at full scale. Roughly what SQNR does it give for a signal 40 dB below full scale, and why?

The error power stays fixed while the signal power falls.

About 10 dB. The quantization error power stays near Δ²/12 while the signal power drops by 40 dB, so SQNR falls by the same 40 dB.

2. Why does companding cost some SQNR for full-scale signals?

Compare the input step sizes near the peaks for the two quantizers.

The compressor spends many levels near zero, so its steps near full scale are wider than the uniform quantizer’s. A full-scale signal sees those wider steps and more error.
